question: Starting July 1, 2026, what is the total (aggregate) Direct Unsubsidized Loan limit for a professional student (e.g., law or medical school) who does not qualify for the interim exception?
answer:
A professional student who doesn't qualify for the interim exception has a $200,000 aggregate limit on unsubsidized loans, minus any amount received as a graduate student [3][4]. This limit doesn't include loans received for undergraduate study [4]. Separately, the new $257,500 lifetime maximum applies to all Title IV loans, including those from undergraduate study [1][4].

The pre-July 2026 aggregate limit was $138,500, and it included undergraduate loans [3]. Grad PLUS loans are no longer available to professional borrowers who don't qualify for the exception [3][4].

A June 24, 2026 court order preliminarily stayed part of the Department's professional degree definition, so whether your program counts as "professional" may differ from the original list. Check with your school [3][4].

studyNotes.focus: The question asks for the aggregate Direct Unsubsidized Loan limit for professional students without the interim exception, starting July 1, 2026.

keyPoints.text: For professional students not eligible for the interim exception, the new annual Unsubsidized Loan limit is $50,000, up from $20,500.
The professional student aggregate limit for those ineligible for the interim exception is $200,000 minus any amount received as a graduate student.
Professional students who qualify for the interim exception keep the pre-OBBBA $138,500 (or $224,000 for eligible health programs) aggregate limit while the exception applies.
Students not enrolled as of June 30, 2026 do not start over; previously borrowed Title IV loans count toward the new aggregate limits.
Direct PLUS Loans for professional borrowers are no longer available to those ineligible for the interim exception.

conflicts.text: Source 3 says the professional aggregate is $200,000 minus prior graduate receipts, while the new professional aggregate in source 2 is only described as applying after the exception period without a figure.

mayBeStale.text: Source 3 notes a June 24, 2026 court stay on part of the professional degree definition, which may change which programs count as professional.
Source 1 is dated May 20, 2026 and source 5 is from March 2026, both predating the final rule and later page updates.
